aboriginal: Continuous song traditions reaching back tens of thousands of years; placed at the left edge of the axis.
vedic: Oldest continuously performed chant tradition; placed at the left edge of the axis.
mesop: The Hurrian hymns from Ugarit (c. 1400 BCE) are the oldest substantially notated music known.
impression: Debussy heard a Javanese gamelan at the 1889 Paris Exposition.
brass: European military bands took drums, cymbals and the march idea from the Ottoman Janissary band.
psych: The Beatles and the Byrds drew on Hindustani raga and sitar in 1965–66.
soca: Lord Shorty built soca by mixing calypso with Indo-Trinidadian rhythms.
hiphop: DJ Kool Herc brought the Jamaican sound-system approach to Bronx block parties.
roma: The Roma migrated from northern India and reached Europe by around 1400.
minimal: Riley, Reich and Glass studied Indian classical music and West African and Balinese drumming.
cumbia: African drumming meets Indigenous gaita flutes on Colombia’s Caribbean coast.
gnawa: Ritual music of Moroccans descended from West African slaves.
fado: Fado drew on the lundu and modinha that travelled from Brazil to Lisbon.
nhacvang: Saigon’s “yellow music” took the bolero rhythm; Vietnamese bolero is still a living style.
balada: A sentimental pop form derived from the bolero, dominant across Latin America from the 1960s.
lukthung: The first recording usually cited is “Mae Saao Chaao Rai” (1938); the name dates from 1964.
champeta: Built on Congolese and other African records played on Cartagena’s picó sound systems.
chamame: Roots in Guaraní dances, the schottische and the Paraguayan polka.
zamacueca: Born in colonial Lima; it became Chile’s cueca and Peru’s marinera.
pacreggae: Herbs, formed in Auckland in 1979, are usually credited as the pioneers.
hawaiian: The guitar reached Hawaii with Mexican and Spanish vaqueros in the 1800s.
citypop: Its principal parent here is AOR, not kayōkyoku: the sound is closer to Los Angeles than to Tokyo’s earlier pop.
kizomba: Angolan semba slowed down and crossed with Antillean zouk.
